newsitem.title: UK: Euro Crude Outlook - Iraq uncertainty dominates.
newsitem.headline: Euro Crude Outlook - Iraq uncertainty dominates.

text.p: European crude markets faced an uncertain start to the week, awaiting clarity on negotiations between the United Nations and Iraq, traders said.
A deal between the U.N. and Baghdad on an aid distribution deal should clear the way for crude exports that will sharply depress prices in the Mediterranean and Europe, traders said.
But at the beginning of the trading week it was unclear if any agreement had been reached.
Dealers were increasingly worried about further delays to Iraqi exports, on hold since end-May, which would sharply boost values.
Many were said to be taking a strong precautionary interest in early August barrels.
If Baghdad does give the go-ahead for exports under the oil-for-food plan Iraqi crude will swamp Mediterranean markets parched of sour crude supply.

Iraq's oil minister predicted in late June that exports would restart at the rate of 730-750,000 barrels per day but others reckon a target of a million bpd will be needed to meet the cash target of $2.14 billion.
The Kirkuk blend, when it eventually appears at the Turkish port of Ceyhan, will ease the tightness of the Med market.
That has has boosted prices of Russian Urals from -$1.40 a barrel at the start of June to around -65 cents.
The effect may be mitigated in the short-term by further logistical and political delays in restarting exports and by tight North Sea crude loading programmes in August.
And dealers were dubious that Iraq would rush crude to the market, pointing out that Baghdad, not the U.N., had insisted the aid plan be finished before sales resume.
"The fact that Iraq has not been exporting when they were allowed to export is a very bullish signal for the oil market," said one trader.
Med traders will also be looking to the results of Turkey's tender for 300,000 tonnes of crude oil, due late on Monday.

The tender paralysed trade in the Med last week and held prices high, hitting refinery margins hard. Its conclusion will free trade in the few Russian Urals barrels left for July as prices slip to 70 or 80 cents under dated Brent.
Whatever comes out of Iraq North Sea crude traders were bullish, pointing to hefty oil field maintenance programmes in August that will trim supply.
A Reuters survey showed a daily shortfall of 245,000 barrels in August from July.
Work at BP's Magnus field and Shell Expro's Brent Bravo platform is due to cut four cargoes from the Brent loading programme.
Work in the Norwegian sector will cut 5.24 million barrels from August liftings, with a two-week shut down at the Statfjord B platform cutting 2.1 million barrels of output.

Early loading schedules showed the Oseberg crude system loading 19.32 million barrels in August, down from 20.4 million in July, while Norway's Statfjord will load 28 855,000 barrel cargoes, including two held over from July.

"Indications are that the market is still strong," said one trader. "Some companies were caught out by the Iraq uncertainty and moved too late last month. They don't want to get caught out this time and will move early."

Differentials on most North Sea grades should stay strong but Dated Brent's high premium over August paper last week has eased. A ULCC cargo play to the U.S. Gulf boosted numbers which then faded in the vessel's wake.

Traders downplayed the effect of the imminent sale of German oil reserves to help Bonn meet the cost of winning entry to a single currency, saying the amounts were not large enough to be particularly bearish.
-- Sean Maguire, London newsroom +44 171 542 8060
